statement: A bakery's site has a home page, a menu page and an order page, all linked together. Together they make one website.
explanation: A website is a set of connected webpages.

statement: A dog groomer's site has five pages: home, prices, gallery, about and contact. Each of these pages is a separate website.
explanation: They are five webpages inside one website.

statement: A school's site has a page for each year group. A parent can go from the Year 7 page to the Year 8 page without leaving the site.
explanation: The pages are connected, so they belong to one website.

statement: A photographer posts one picture on a friend's blog. That one picture is the photographer's website.
explanation: A website is her own set of connected pages; one picture on someone else's blog is not.

statement: A football club's website shows match dates, players and tickets. Fans can find all of these in one place.
explanation: Connecting the pages in one site lets fans find everything together.

statement: A cinema's site shows film times on one page and ticket prices on another. The two pages are the same webpage.
explanation: They are two different webpages in one website.

statement: On a museum's site, each exhibition has its own page with photos and opening times. Each exhibition page is one webpage.
explanation: Each is a single page inside the larger website.

statement: A pizza shop puts its menu, its prices and its opening hours on one webpage. This means the shop has three websites.
explanation: One webpage is part of one website; three kinds of information do not make three websites.

statement: A band's website has a separate webpage for each album. Fans can open the page for the album they want.
explanation: Splitting content into webpages helps visitors find one album at a time.

statement: A charity puts its address only on its Contact page. A visitor can read the address on every webpage of the site.
explanation: If it is only on the Contact page, it is not on every webpage.

statement: A zoo's homepage shows a big photo of a tiger and buttons for tickets, animals and maps. The homepage helps visitors decide where to go next.
explanation: The homepage introduces the site and points to its main parts.

statement: A shoe shop's homepage is usually the last page a customer sees, after paying.
explanation: The homepage is the main page; visitors usually see it first.

statement: A library's homepage says "Welcome to Riverside Library" at the top. Visitors know at once whose site they are on.
explanation: A homepage introduces the site and its owner.

statement: A bike repair shop's homepage is full of tiny text, with no pictures and no buttons. The homepage makes it easy for visitors to find what they need.
explanation: With only tiny text and no buttons, visitors will struggle to find their way.

statement: A swimming pool's homepage shows today's opening times near the top. This is useful, because many visitors only want to know when it is open.
explanation: Putting the most wanted information on the homepage saves visitors time.

statement: A florist's homepage has three sections: new flowers, weddings and delivery. The three sections are three different websites.
explanation: They are three parts of one page.

statement: A recipe page has one section for the ingredients and another for the steps. Splitting the page into sections makes the recipe easier to follow.
explanation: Clear sections help readers find what they need.

statement: A long page about a school trip has no sections, just one long block of text. Visitors will probably find information on it quickly.
explanation: One long block with no sections is slow to search.

statement: A sports club page has a "Results" section and a "Next match" section. A fan who only wants the score can go straight to the right section.
explanation: Sections let visitors jump to the part they need.

statement: A café website puts its prices, its history and its staff photos in the same section. This makes each kind of information easy to find.
explanation: Mixing different content in one section makes each part harder to find.

statement: A games shop's website has prices, photos of games and short reviews. All of these are the site's content.
explanation: Content means the information, images and other material on a site.

statement: A nature website has lovely colours and buttons but no articles, photos or facts. The site has a lot of content.
explanation: Colours and buttons are design; without information or images there is little content.

statement: A news website adds new stories every morning. Fresh content gives readers a reason to come back.
explanation: New content means there is something new to read on each visit.

statement: A dentist's website still shows its Christmas opening times in June. Its content is up to date.
explanation: Christmas times in June show that the content is out of date.

statement: A travel site's content includes videos of beaches as well as written guides. Content can be more than words.
explanation: Images, videos and sound are all content.

statement: On a cinema site, the heading "Now showing" is in tiny grey letters at the bottom of the page. The heading is easy to notice.
explanation: Tiny grey letters at the bottom are easy to miss; headings need to stand out.

statement: A charity page has the heading "How your money helps" above a list of projects. The heading tells readers what the section is about.
explanation: A heading introduces the content below it.

statement: A recipe site uses the heading "Click here" above its list of ingredients. The heading tells readers clearly what is below it.
explanation: "Click here" says nothing about ingredients; "Ingredients" would be clearer.

statement: A school website's headings are big and bold, and the text under them is smaller. Visitors can see where each new topic starts.
explanation: Bigger, bolder headings mark the start of each part.

statement: A pet shop page has no headings, only long paragraphs. Readers can probably find the part about cat food straight away.
explanation: Without headings, readers have to read everything to find one topic.

statement: Under the heading "Our animals", a zoo page has the subheadings "Big cats", "Birds" and "Reptiles". The subheadings split the topic into smaller parts.
explanation: Subheadings divide a section into smaller groups.

statement: On a shop page, the subheading is bigger and bolder than the main heading. This makes it clear which one is more important.
explanation: A subheading should be smaller than the heading; making it bigger confuses the order.

statement: A long article about a school play uses subheadings such as "The cast" and "Behind the scenes". The subheadings help readers find the part they want.
explanation: Smaller titles break a long article into easy-to-find parts.

statement: A gaming website puts the subheading "Prices" above a section about the history of the company. The subheading matches the content.
explanation: "Prices" does not describe company history, so it misleads readers.

statement: A recipe page uses the subheadings "You will need" and "Method". Even a quick reader can see how the recipe is organised.
explanation: Clear subheadings show the structure at a glance.

statement: A bakery's homepage shows a photo of burnt, flat bread. The image makes the bakery look skilled.
explanation: Burnt, flat bread makes the bakery look careless.

statement: An adventure park's website shows a photo of children laughing on a zip wire. The image shows visitors the fun they could have.
explanation: The photo lets visitors imagine themselves there.

statement: A hotel's website uses the same tiny, blurry photo of a bed on every page. The images help visitors see what the rooms are like.
explanation: Tiny, blurry photos hide what the rooms look like.

statement: A clothes shop shows each jacket from the front, the back and the side. More images help shoppers decide.
explanation: Seeing the jacket from different sides answers shoppers' questions.

statement: A science museum uses pictures of dinosaurs on its page about space. The images match the content well.
explanation: Dinosaurs do not match a page about space.

statement: Under a photo of a smiling runner, the caption says "Mia finishes her first marathon". The caption tells us who she is and what she did.
explanation: A caption explains what the image shows.

statement: A football club posts a team photo with no caption. Visitors can easily learn each player's name from the photo.
explanation: Without a caption, the photo does not tell visitors the players' names.

statement: A museum's gallery page gives each painting a caption with its name and date. The captions help visitors understand what they are looking at.
explanation: Captions add facts that the picture alone cannot show.

statement: A caption under a photo of a cake says "Our new bike repair service". The caption explains the image well.
explanation: The caption is about bikes, not the cake, so it does not match.

statement: A charity puts the caption "The new well in Kito village, 2026" under a photo. The caption tells visitors where the money went.
explanation: It explains what the image shows and where.

statement: A sports shop's logo is a huge, detailed painting with lots of tiny people in it. The logo will be easy to recognise when it is small.
explanation: A detailed picture is hard to recognise when it is shrunk; simple logos work best.

statement: A coffee shop's logo, a cup with a heart, appears in the top corner of every page. Visitors always know which site they are on.
explanation: Showing the logo on every page reminds visitors whose site it is.

statement: A charity uses a different logo on each page of its website. This helps people recognise the charity.
explanation: Changing the logo again and again makes the charity harder to recognise.

statement: A dog-walking business uses a paw print as its logo. The logo suggests what the business does.
explanation: A paw print makes people think of dogs.

statement: A bank's logo is a cartoon clown with a squeaky red nose. The logo makes the bank look serious and safe.
explanation: A cartoon clown looks silly, not serious.

statement: An illustrator's website shows twenty of her best drawings with short notes. The site is a portfolio of her work.
explanation: A portfolio is a collection showing someone's work.

statement: A photographer's portfolio shows only photos taken by other people. The portfolio shows what the photographer can do.
explanation: Other people's photos say nothing about her own skills.

statement: A student puts his best design projects from Year 7 to Year 9 on one website, in order. The portfolio shows how his skills have grown.
explanation: Putting work in order shows progress over time.

statement: A cake maker's portfolio shows her best cakes, her worst cakes and some cakes she did not make. This makes the portfolio stronger.
explanation: A portfolio should show her own best work.

statement: An architect's portfolio groups his buildings into "Homes", "Schools" and "Parks". This makes his work easier to explore.
explanation: Grouping the work helps visitors find what interests them.

statement: A wedding photographer's gallery has one photo in it. Visitors can see a wide range of her work.
explanation: One photo cannot show a wide range.

statement: A zoo's gallery page shows rows of small animal photos that get bigger when you choose one. Visitors can look through many pictures quickly.
explanation: A gallery collects many images in one place.

statement: A school's art gallery page shows the pupils' paintings as a list of titles, with no pictures. The page works well as a gallery.
explanation: A gallery should show the images; a list of titles does not.

statement: A skate park's gallery shows photos from last summer's competition. The gallery shows visitors what happens at the park.
explanation: Photos of real events help visitors picture the place.

statement: A furniture shop puts its delivery prices in its gallery. This is where most visitors will expect to find them.
explanation: Visitors expect a gallery to hold pictures, not prices.

statement: A restaurant's website has a menu at the top with "Food", "Book a table" and "Find us". The menu shows visitors the main places they can go.
explanation: A menu is a list of choices or places to go.

statement: A library hides its website menu at the very bottom of each long page. Visitors will find the menu straight away.
explanation: Visitors usually look for a menu at the top; at the bottom of a long page it is easy to miss.

statement: A game studio's menu has five short choices: Games, News, Jobs, About and Contact. A short menu is easy to read.
explanation: A few clear choices are quick to scan.

statement: A hardware shop's menu has fifty choices in one long row. The menu is easy to use.
explanation: Fifty choices are too many to read quickly.

statement: On a phone, a museum's menu is hidden behind a small button with three lines. Tapping the button opens the full menu.
explanation: Hiding the menu saves space on small screens.

statement: A hotel website has no menu, no links and no buttons between pages. Visitors can easily move around the site.
explanation: Without navigation features, there is no way to move between pages.

statement: A theme park site has a menu, a search bar and a "Back to top" button. All three are part of the site's navigation.
explanation: They are all features that help visitors move around.

statement: On a school website, the navigation moves to a different place on each page. This helps visitors find their way.
explanation: Moving navigation confuses visitors; it should stay in the same place.

statement: A shop website shows "Home > Shoes > Trainers" at the top of a page. This navigation shows visitors where they are in the site.
explanation: The path shows which part of the site the page belongs to.

statement: A hospital's website uses the navigation labels "Stuff", "Things" and "More". These labels tell visitors exactly where each link goes.
explanation: Vague labels don't say what is behind each link. On a hospital site, visitors need clear labels such as "Appointments" or "Find us".

statement: A news story about a flood includes a link to a page of safety advice. The link takes readers to more help.
explanation: A link takes you to another place when you select it.

statement: A charity page has a link that says "Donate", but it opens a page about the charity's history. The link works well.
explanation: A link should go where its label promises.

statement: A recipe page links the word "pastry" to another recipe for making pastry. Readers can learn the extra step if they need it.
explanation: The link connects related content.

statement: A school page shows its links in the same colour as normal text, with no underline. Visitors can easily tell which words are links.
explanation: Links that look like normal text are hard to spot.

statement: A cinema site's "Buy tickets" link goes straight to the booking page. The link saves visitors time.
explanation: A clear link takes visitors directly where they want to go.

statement: A shop's "Add to basket" button is tiny and pale grey, hidden among the text. The button is easy to find.
explanation: A tiny, pale button hidden in text is easy to miss.

statement: A gym website has a big orange button that says "Join today". The button makes the main action clear.
explanation: A clear, bright button shows visitors what to do.

statement: A form's button says only "Go". Every visitor will understand exactly what the button does.
explanation: "Go" is unclear; "Send message" would say what happens.

statement: A music site's play button shows a small triangle. Most visitors understand the symbol without any words.
explanation: The triangle is a familiar symbol for "play".

statement: On a pizza site, the "Order now" button does nothing when you click it. The button helps customers to order.
explanation: A button that does nothing stops customers from ordering.

statement: A family farm's About page tells the story of three generations growing apples. The page helps visitors trust the business.
explanation: Learning who runs the farm makes it feel real and trustworthy.

statement: A bakery's About page lists only the prices of its cakes. The page explains who the bakers are.
explanation: Prices do not tell visitors who the bakers are.

statement: A young designer's About page has her photo and a short paragraph about why she loves design. Visitors learn a little about her.
explanation: An About page explains who a person is and what they do.

statement: A charity's About page is three screens long, with no headings and no photos. Most visitors will read all of it.
explanation: Long, unbroken text is likely to put visitors off.

statement: A climbing centre's About page says when it opened and what makes it different. This information belongs on the About page.
explanation: The About page explains who an organisation is and what it does.

statement: A vet's Contact page has no phone number, no email and no address. Visitors can easily get in touch.
explanation: With no contact details, visitors cannot get in touch.

statement: A plumber's Contact page shows a phone number, an email form and a map. Customers can choose how to reach him.
explanation: Offering several ways to get in touch helps different customers.

statement: A cinema puts its phone number on its About page and nowhere else. Most visitors will look for it there first.
explanation: Most visitors look for contact details on the Contact page.

statement: A music teacher's Contact page says "I reply within 24 hours." This tells visitors what to expect.
explanation: Saying how quickly she replies helps visitors feel confident.

statement: A shop's Contact page can only be reached from a small link at the bottom of its Privacy page. The Contact page is easy to find.
explanation: A link hidden on one page is hard to find.

statement: A museum's header shows its logo on the left and its main menu on the right. The header stays the same on every page.
explanation: The header often holds the logo and main navigation across the site.

statement: A shoe shop's header is at the very bottom of the page, under the copyright line. This is where visitors expect a header.
explanation: The header is the area across the top of a page.

statement: A news site's header shows the site's name and today's date. Readers see them before anything else.
explanation: The header is at the top, so it is seen first.

statement: A clothing site's header is so tall that it fills the whole phone screen. Visitors can see the clothes straight away.
explanation: A huge header pushes the clothes off the screen.

statement: A theatre's header has a "Book tickets" button next to the menu. Visitors can book from any page.
explanation: Putting the button in the header makes it available everywhere.

statement: A bank puts its main "Log in" button only in the footer of a very long page. Customers will find it quickly.
explanation: Important buttons in the footer of a long page are easy to miss.

statement: A café's footer lists its address, opening hours and social media links. Visitors who scroll to the bottom find useful details.
explanation: The footer often holds contact details and links.

statement: A toy shop's footer is the first thing visitors see when a page opens.
explanation: The footer is at the bottom, so it is usually one of the last things visitors see.

statement: A charity's footer shows its official charity number. Visitors who want to check that it is real can find the number there.
explanation: Small but important details often sit in the footer.

statement: A gaming site's footer copies the header exactly: logo and main menu, nothing else. This is what a footer usually contains.
explanation: Footers usually hold extra links and contact details, not just a copy of the header.

statement: A toy shop's website is used mostly by parents buying presents. Its visitors are adults, even though the toys are for children.
explanation: The people using the site are the ones who buy, not the ones who play.

statement: A website for retired people uses tiny grey text and fast flashing pictures. The design suits its visitors.
explanation: Many older visitors need larger, clearer text and calmer pages.

statement: A museum finds that most visitors to its website use phones. The museum should check that its pages work well on small screens.
explanation: Knowing which devices visitors use helps designers make good choices.

statement: A nursery school's website is written in long, technical words. The writing suits its users, who are busy parents.
explanation: Busy parents want short, clear information, not technical words.

statement: A cooking site asks users what they think of each recipe. Listening to users can help the site improve.
explanation: Users' opinions show what works and what doesn't.

statement: The purpose of a charity's website is to raise money, but the "Donate" button is hidden at the bottom of one page. The design supports the purpose.
explanation: Hiding the main action works against the site's purpose.

statement: A cinema's website is mainly there to sell tickets. Putting "Buy tickets" on every film page supports its purpose.
explanation: Each film page leads straight to the main goal.

statement: A school website's purpose is to inform parents, but most of its pages are adverts for other companies. The content matches the purpose.
explanation: Adverts do not inform parents about the school.

statement: An artist's website has one main purpose: to show her work to galleries. Large, clear images of her paintings help it do that.
explanation: Good images serve the purpose of showing her work.

statement: A train company's website plays a full-screen video before visitors can check train times. This probably helps the site's main purpose.
explanation: Most visitors want times quickly; a video in the way slows them down.

statement: On a phone, visitors tap instead of clicking, so buttons need to be big enough for a finger.
explanation: Fingers are bigger than a mouse pointer, so small buttons are hard to tap.

statement: A shop's links are so close together that visitors often tap the wrong one. The links are easy to tap on a phone.
explanation: Links that are too close together cause wrong taps.

statement: A quiz site lets students tap an answer to see if it is right. Each tap gets a quick reply.
explanation: Tapping is how visitors select something on a touch screen.

statement: On a recipe site, visitors click six times to reach one recipe. The recipe is quick to reach.
explanation: Six clicks is slow; good sites keep important pages close.

statement: A photo site lets visitors click a picture to see it bigger. The click gives them more detail when they want it.
explanation: Clicking selects the picture and opens a larger view.

statement: A café's opening times are at the very bottom of a long homepage. Visitors can see them without scrolling.
explanation: At the bottom of a long page, visitors must scroll to find them.

statement: A story site lets readers scroll down through a long article on their phone. Scrolling is a natural way to read on a phone.
explanation: Moving down a page with a thumb is easy on a phone.

statement: A website makes visitors scroll sideways to read each line of text. This makes reading comfortable.
explanation: Scrolling sideways for every line is tiring and awkward.

statement: A news page adds more stories as the reader scrolls down. Visitors keep reading without opening a new page.
explanation: Scrolling loads more content on the same page.

statement: A shop's "Buy now" button is at the bottom of a page that needs ten screens of scrolling. Most shoppers will easily see it.
explanation: Many shoppers will stop scrolling before they reach it.

statement: A bookshop's website lets visitors browse books by type: mystery, sport, fantasy. This lets visitors look around even if they don't know what they want.
explanation: Browsing means looking through content without a fixed aim.

statement: A clothes site shows one product at a time, with no way to see the others. The site makes browsing easy.
explanation: With one item at a time and no way to see others, browsing is hard.

statement: A museum's online collection lets visitors browse paintings by century. This helps curious visitors explore.
explanation: Grouping by century gives a clear way to look around.

statement: A shopper who knows exactly which trainers she wants will probably browse every category first.
explanation: She will probably search for them directly instead of browsing.

statement: A music app suggests "If you like this, try…" under each song. The suggestions encourage users to keep browsing.
explanation: Suggestions give users more to look through.

statement: A school puts its timetable online as a file to download. Once downloaded, the timetable can only be read on the school website.
explanation: A downloaded file is saved on your device and can be opened there.

statement: A music teacher's site lets students download practice sheets. They then print them at home.
explanation: Downloading saves the file to their device.

statement: A game studio's site starts a huge download as soon as the homepage opens, without asking. Visitors will be pleased.
explanation: Unexpected downloads can worry visitors and use up their data.

statement: A recipe site offers a "Download as PDF" button. Cooks then have the recipe even without the internet.
explanation: A downloaded file can be opened offline.

statement: A charity's "Download our report" link opens a page that says "File not found". The download works well.
explanation: "File not found" means the download has failed.

statement: A competition page has a "Submit your photo" button. Pressing it sends the photo to the organisers.
explanation: Submitting sends information to the site.

statement: On a booking form, the "Submit" button is greyed out until the boxes are filled. This stops visitors from sending a complete booking.
explanation: It stops incomplete bookings; once the boxes are filled, the booking can be sent.

statement: After a visitor submits a question, the page says "Thanks! We'll reply soon." The message shows the question was sent.
explanation: The message confirms that the submission worked.

statement: A survey's submit button is labelled "Cancel". Visitors will know that this button sends their answers.
explanation: "Cancel" suggests stopping, not sending.

statement: A school's homework site lets students submit work online before midnight. This saves them a trip to school.
explanation: Students can send their work from home.

statement: A bakery prints the URL "www.bluebun-bakery-online-official-site-2026.com" on its bags. The URL is short and easy to remember.
explanation: It is long and hard to remember.

statement: A band uses the URL "www.thelanternband.com". The URL matches the band's name, so fans find it easily.
explanation: A URL that matches the name is easy to guess and remember.

statement: On a zoo's website, the page about penguins and the page about lions have exactly the same URL.
explanation: Each webpage has its own address.

statement: A visitor copies the URL of a recipe and sends it to a friend. The friend opens the same recipe.
explanation: A URL is the address of the page.

statement: A fake website copies a bank's design but uses a slightly different URL. The URL is the same as the real bank's.
explanation: A slightly different URL is a sign the site is not the real bank.

statement: A sports club's navigation bar runs across the top of every page with links to Fixtures, Teams and Shop. Fans can jump to any main part of the site.
explanation: A navigation bar links to the main parts of a site.

statement: A hotel's navigation bar has different links on each page. This makes the site easier to use.
explanation: Changing links confuse visitors; a navigation bar should stay the same.

statement: A long shop page keeps its navigation bar at the top, even as visitors scroll down. Visitors never have to scroll back up to move to another section.
explanation: A navigation bar that stays visible is always ready to use.

statement: A navigation bar with fifteen links squeezed into one line is easy to read on a phone.
explanation: Fifteen links in one line are tiny and hard to tap on a phone.

statement: A college's navigation bar puts "Apply" on the far right in a different colour. The design makes the most important link stand out.
explanation: A different colour draws attention to the main action.

statement: A shoe shop's dropdown menu opens and closes so fast that visitors cannot choose an option. The menu is easy to use.
explanation: If it closes too fast, visitors cannot pick anything.

statement: On a university site, pointing at "Courses" opens a dropdown menu of subjects. The menu shows more choices without filling the page.
explanation: A dropdown hides extra options until they are needed.

statement: A form asks visitors to choose their country from a dropdown menu of 200 countries in random order. Finding your country will be quick.
explanation: Random order makes a long list very slow to search.

statement: A travel site's dropdown menu lets visitors choose how many adults and children are going. Visitors pick from a list instead of typing.
explanation: Choosing from a list prevents typing mistakes.

statement: A dropdown menu on a bakery site contains a single option. The dropdown saves visitors time.
explanation: With one option, a dropdown adds a step for nothing.

statement: A huge online shop puts a search bar at the top of every page. This helps shoppers who know what they want to find it fast.
explanation: Typing a word is quicker than browsing thousands of products.

statement: A recipe site's search bar finds nothing when visitors type "chocolate cake", even though the site has three chocolate cake recipes. The search bar works well.
explanation: If it misses recipes that are there, it is not working well.

statement: A library site's search bar suggests titles as you type. This helps visitors who are not sure of the spelling.
explanation: Suggestions help visitors find items even with small mistakes.

statement: A band's three-page website makes a big search bar its main feature. A search bar is the most useful thing on such a small site.
explanation: With only three pages, simple navigation is enough; search adds little.

statement: A school site's search bar is a small box with a magnifying glass icon. Most visitors recognise the icon at once.
explanation: The magnifying glass is a common symbol for search.

statement: A music app uses a picture of a banana as its "play" icon. Users will understand the icon straight away.
explanation: A banana is not a familiar symbol for "play"; a triangle is.

statement: A shop shows a small trolley icon with a number on it. It shows shoppers how many items are in their basket.
explanation: The icon stands for the basket, and the number adds information.

statement: A website uses ten different icons for "home" on different pages. This helps visitors learn what the icon means.
explanation: One icon used every time is much easier to learn.

statement: A weather site uses a sun, a cloud and a raindrop icon for each day. Visitors understand the forecast in a second.
explanation: Simple icons communicate quickly.

statement: A form uses an icon with no label for "Delete your account". Users can be sure exactly what it does.
explanation: An unlabelled icon for an important action can easily be misunderstood.

statement: A dentist's booking form asks only for a name, a phone number and a preferred day. A short form is quick to fill in.
explanation: Fewer questions mean visitors finish faster.

statement: A newsletter sign-up form asks for your name, email, address, phone number, birthday and job. The form is quick and simple.
explanation: Six questions just to get a newsletter is long and off-putting.

statement: A school trip form shows a red message when the parent forgets the child's name. The form helps people fix mistakes.
explanation: The message shows what is missing.

statement: A form deletes everything the visitor has typed after one small mistake. This makes the form pleasant to use.
explanation: Losing all the information is frustrating.

statement: A charity's volunteer form groups its questions under "About you" and "Your free time". The groups make the form easier to follow.
explanation: Grouping related questions makes the form clearer.

statement: An input field for a phone number is wide enough to show just three digits. Visitors can easily check what they have typed.
explanation: They cannot see the whole number, so mistakes are hard to spot.

statement: An input field shows "e.g. sam@school.org" in pale grey before you type. The example shows what to write.
explanation: A hint inside the field guides visitors.

statement: A form has one input field labelled "Details". Visitors will know exactly what to type.
explanation: "Details" is too vague to guide visitors.

statement: On a phone, tapping the input field for a phone number opens a keypad with numbers. This makes typing easier.
explanation: The right keyboard suits the input field.

statement: A sign-up page has input fields with no labels, just empty boxes. Visitors can tell which box is for their email.
explanation: Without labels, visitors have to guess.

statement: A pizza site lets customers tick checkboxes for extra toppings. They choose as many as they like.
explanation: Checkboxes allow more than one choice.

statement: A form shows a checkbox that is already ticked for "Send me adverts every day". This puts the visitor fully in control.
explanation: A box ticked in advance makes the choice for them, and they may not notice it.

statement: A competition form has a checkbox saying "I agree to the rules". Entrants must tick it before they can submit.
explanation: The checkbox records that they agree.

statement: A cinema form lists "popcorn", "drink" and "ice cream" as checkboxes. Customers can choose only one of them.
explanation: Checkboxes let customers choose as many as they want.

statement: A tiny checkbox is hard to tick on a phone. Letting visitors tap the words next to it as well can help.
explanation: A bigger target is easier to tap.

statement: A news site puts its main story in a narrow sidebar and adverts in the wide main column. The main story gets the attention it needs.
explanation: The main story belongs in the main column; a narrow sidebar is for extra content.

statement: A blog has a sidebar listing its most popular posts. It gives readers more to read after one article.
explanation: A sidebar holds extra links beside the main content.

statement: On a phone, a wide sidebar squeezes the main text into a thin strip. The text is easy to read.
explanation: A squeezed column of text is hard to read on a small screen.

statement: A recipe site's sidebar shows a shopping list for the recipe. Cooks see it while they read the steps.
explanation: The sidebar gives extra, useful information beside the main content.

statement: A sidebar on a children's game site is packed with flashing adverts. This helps children focus on the game.
explanation: Flashing adverts pull attention away from the game.

statement: A video site shows a small thumbnail for each video. Visitors choose which video to watch from its picture.
explanation: A thumbnail is a small preview that opens the full item.

statement: A portfolio shows huge full-size images instead of thumbnails, so each picture fills the screen. Visitors can compare many projects at once.
explanation: Full-size images show one at a time; thumbnails let visitors compare many.

statement: A shop's thumbnails open a larger photo when tapped. The page loads quickly but still offers detail.
explanation: Small previews load fast; the large photo appears only when wanted.

statement: A video's thumbnail shows an exciting explosion that never happens in the video. The thumbnail is an honest preview.
explanation: A thumbnail showing something that is not in the video is misleading.

statement: A news site chooses a close-up of a worried face as the thumbnail for a story. The thumbnail can make people want to click.
explanation: An emotional face draws attention and curiosity.

statement: A cooking site shows a video of the recipe, but visitors must leave the site to watch it. The video is embedded media.
explanation: Embedded media plays inside the webpage; this video makes visitors leave.

statement: A band's website plays a song sample inside the page. Fans listen without leaving the site.
explanation: The audio is embedded in the page.

statement: A history page embeds ten videos that start playing loudly at the same time. This makes the page pleasant to use.
explanation: Ten videos playing at once is noisy and confusing.

statement: A museum page embeds a map showing where it is. Visitors plan their trip without opening another app.
explanation: An embedded map is useful content inside the page.

statement: A school page embeds a video that is too wide for phone screens, so half of it is cut off. Embedded media like this suits phone users.
explanation: A video that is cut off on phones does not suit phone users.

statement: An advert for a summer camp links to a landing page with dates, prices and a "Book now" button. The page gives visitors what the advert promised.
explanation: A landing page is where visitors arrive after an advert.

statement: A trainer advert promises "50% off today", but its landing page shows full prices and no sale. The landing page matches the advert.
explanation: The landing page breaks the advert's promise.

statement: A charity's campaign landing page has one message and one button: "Give £5". The page keeps visitors focused.
explanation: One clear action makes the page effective.

statement: A game's advert leads to the company's homepage, where visitors have to search for the game. This is a strong landing page for the advert.
explanation: Visitors have to search, so the page does not continue the advert's message.

statement: A book's landing page shows the cover, a short review and a "Buy" button. Visitors who click the advert can act straight away.
explanation: Everything they need is on the first page they see.

statement: A product page uses tabs for "Description", "Sizes" and "Reviews". Clicking a tab takes the visitor to a different website.
explanation: Tabs switch content on the same page; visitors stay where they are.

statement: A recipe page uses two tabs: "Ingredients" and "Method". Cooks switch between them without scrolling.
explanation: Tabs show different sections in the same space.

statement: On a football club page, the match times are hidden behind a tab labelled "More". Fans will find the match times quickly.
explanation: A vague label hides important information.

statement: A phone shop page uses tabs to compare three phone models. Shoppers can switch quickly without leaving the page.
explanation: Tabs let visitors move between related sections easily.

statement: A page has twelve tabs in one row on a phone screen, each with tiny text. The tabs are easy to read and tap.
explanation: Twelve tiny tabs on a phone are hard to read and tap.

statement: A vegan café uses leaf greens, recycled-paper textures and the line "Good food, good planet" across its site. The branding links the café with caring for the environment.
explanation: Each choice points to nature and sustainability.

statement: A luxury watch brand's website uses cartoon fonts, bright clashing colours and jokes. The branding suits an expensive, serious product.
explanation: Playful, cheap-looking choices clash with an expensive product.

statement: A sports brand uses the same bold orange and the same short slogans on its website, its app and its shop windows. Strong branding like this helps people recognise it anywhere.
explanation: Repeating the same choices everywhere builds recognition.

statement: A children's library uses black, grey and a heavy, formal font on its website. The branding makes the library feel fun and welcoming for young readers.
explanation: Dark colours and a formal font feel serious, not fun.

statement: A wedding photographer's branding is calm: soft colours, plenty of space and short sentences. The branding suggests she is relaxed and professional.
explanation: Calm design choices create a calm, professional impression.

statement: A bakery uses a different logo, different colours and a different font on its website, its menu and its van. Its visual identity is clear and recognisable.
explanation: Changing everything makes the identity confusing.

statement: A museum uses the same dark blue, the same thin lettering and the same star symbol on its website and posters. Together these create its visual identity.
explanation: Connected colours, lettering and symbols make the brand visible.

statement: A gym changes its prices and opening times. This changes its visual identity.
explanation: Visual identity is about colours, lettering, images and symbols, not prices or times.

statement: An animal rescue charity replaces its old logo with a simple paw and switches to warm orange. Its visual identity has changed.
explanation: New symbols and colours make a new visual identity.

statement: A new app copies another company's logo and colours exactly. This gives the app a strong, unique visual identity.
explanation: Copying another company's identity makes it neither strong nor unique.

statement: On a college website, every button is the same shape and colour. This consistency helps students know what can be clicked.
explanation: Repeated patterns teach visitors how the site works.

statement: A shop website uses blue links on some pages, red links on others and plain black on the rest. The site is consistent.
explanation: Links that change colour are inconsistent and confusing.

statement: A news site puts the date under the headline in every article. Readers learn where to look.
explanation: A consistent pattern saves readers effort.

statement: A school site has a different menu layout on each page. This makes the site easier to learn.
explanation: Changing layouts make visitors relearn every page.

statement: A design team writes a short guide listing the fonts, colours and button styles for the whole site. The guide helps to keep the site consistent.
explanation: Shared rules keep everyone's pages matching.

statement: A calm meditation app uses a colour palette of flashing red, bright yellow and neon green. The palette suits the app's purpose.
explanation: Bright, flashing colours feel exciting, not calm.

statement: A seaside hotel uses a colour palette of sand, sea-blue and white. The palette reminds visitors of the beach.
explanation: The colours connect the site with its location.

statement: A website uses twelve bright colours on one page, all equally strong. The colour palette makes the page look organised.
explanation: Too many strong colours make a page look busy.

statement: A bank uses a small colour palette of navy, white and one shade of green. The limited palette helps the site look calm and reliable.
explanation: A few steady colours feel trustworthy.

statement: A children's game site uses only dark grey and brown. The colour palette will probably excite young players.
explanation: Dull colours are unlikely to excite children.

statement: A horror film website uses jagged, uneven letters for its title. The typography adds to the scary mood.
explanation: Uneven, sharp letters feel unsettling.

statement: A law firm uses a bubbly cartoon font for all its headings. The typography makes the firm look serious and trustworthy.
explanation: Bubbly cartoon letters look playful, not serious.

statement: A news site uses one font for headlines and another for articles, and keeps to those two. The typography looks organised.
explanation: Two consistent fonts create a sense of order.

statement: A shop's site uses six different fonts on one page. The typography looks calm and professional.
explanation: Too many fonts look messy.

statement: A recipe site sets its steps in large text with plenty of space between the lines. The typography makes the steps easy to follow in a busy kitchen.
explanation: Large, well-spaced text is readable from a distance.

statement: A designer chooses a font whose letters end in small finishing strokes and calls it a sans-serif font.
explanation: Small finishing strokes make it a serif font.

statement: A university uses a serif font for its name to suggest history and tradition.
explanation: Serif fonts are often linked with books, history and tradition.

statement: A playful toy brand chooses an old-fashioned serif font like the ones in old newspapers. The font matches its fun, modern image.
explanation: An old-newspaper serif suggests tradition, not playful fun.

statement: A literary magazine sets its long articles in a serif font. The font gives the pages a bookish feel.
explanation: Serif fonts are common in printed books.

statement: The letters on a gym's website have small decorative strokes at their ends. This makes the font sans-serif.
explanation: Sans-serif means without those strokes; this font is a serif.

statement: A tech company uses a clean sans-serif font across its site. The font helps it look modern.
explanation: Simple letters without strokes feel modern and clean.

statement: A wedding planner who wants an old-fashioned, elegant feel uses a plain sans-serif font for everything. The font perfectly suits the mood.
explanation: An old-fashioned, elegant mood usually suits a serif or script font better.

statement: Many apps use sans-serif fonts because simple letter shapes stay clear on small screens.
explanation: Simple shapes are easy to read at small sizes.

statement: A sans-serif font is chosen for a historical society's website because it looks old and traditional.
explanation: Sans-serif fonts usually look modern; serifs suggest tradition.

statement: A road-safety site uses bold sans-serif headings, like road signs. The style is quick to read at a glance.
explanation: Plain, bold letters are quick to read.

statement: A website puts pale yellow text on a white background. The contrast makes the text easy to read.
explanation: Pale yellow on white has very low contrast.

statement: A cinema site uses white text on a black background. The strong contrast makes film titles stand out.
explanation: Light on dark creates high contrast.

statement: A shop makes its "Buy" button the same colour as the background. The button stands out clearly.
explanation: Without contrast, the button blends in.

statement: A charity uses one bright red button on an otherwise grey page. The contrast draws the eye to the button.
explanation: The one bright colour stands out against the grey.

statement: A school site puts grey text on a slightly lighter grey background. This will be easy for visitors with weak eyesight to read.
explanation: Low contrast makes reading harder, especially with weak eyesight.

statement: A perfume brand's homepage shows one bottle with a lot of empty space around it. The whitespace makes the product feel special.
explanation: Space around an item focuses attention and suggests luxury.

statement: A news site removes the space between its stories to fit more on the screen. The page now feels calm and easy to read.
explanation: Removing space makes the page crowded and harder to read.

statement: A form leaves space between each group of questions. The whitespace shows which questions belong together.
explanation: Gaps separate the groups clearly.

statement: A designer fills every gap on a page with extra pictures and links. This will help visitors focus.
explanation: Removing all whitespace crowds the page and makes focusing harder.

statement: A poetry website leaves wide margins around each poem. The whitespace gives readers room to slow down.
explanation: Space around text creates a calm reading experience.

statement: On a menu page, each dish name starts at a slightly different point on the left. The text is neatly aligned.
explanation: Different starting points mean the text is not aligned.

statement: A portfolio lines up its images along the same left edge. The alignment makes the page look tidy.
explanation: Shared edges create order.

statement: A form's labels and boxes are centred, so their left edges zig-zag down the page. This alignment makes the form quick to scan.
explanation: Zig-zag edges make the eye jump, which slows scanning.

statement: On a shop page, prices are aligned on the right so the numbers line up. Shoppers compare them quickly.
explanation: Lining up numbers makes comparison easy.

statement: A designer moves one heading slightly out of line with everything else by accident. The mistake has no effect on how the page looks.
explanation: Small misalignments make a page look careless.

statement: A recipe site places a photo at the top, the ingredients on the left and the steps on the right. The layout puts what cooks need side by side.
explanation: A clear arrangement helps cooks follow the recipe.

statement: A shop's layout puts the product photo at the bottom and a long legal notice at the top. The layout puts the most important content first.
explanation: The legal notice pushes the product down; the photo should come first.

statement: A news site uses the same layout for each article. Readers know where to find the headline, the date and the story.
explanation: A repeated layout is easy to learn.

statement: A charity page scatters its text boxes randomly across the screen. Visitors will easily know where to start reading.
explanation: A random layout gives visitors no clear starting point.

statement: On phones, a festival site changes its layout from three columns to one. Visitors read without zooming in.
explanation: A single column fits a narrow screen.

statement: A photo gallery places its pictures at random sizes and positions, with no rows or columns. It uses a grid.
explanation: A grid uses rows and columns; random placement does not.

statement: An online shop shows its products in rows of four. The grid makes them easy to compare.
explanation: Equal rows and columns let shoppers scan quickly.

statement: A designer builds a page on a twelve-column grid. The grid makes it harder to line up the images and text.
explanation: A grid gives designers columns to line content up against.

statement: A news homepage uses a grid with one large story and four smaller ones. The grid shows which story matters most.
explanation: Different cell sizes in a grid show importance.

statement: A school site's grid has columns of different widths on each page. The grid creates consistency.
explanation: Changing column widths breaks consistency.

statement: A concert page shows the band's name biggest, the date smaller and the venue smallest. The visual hierarchy tells visitors what to read first.
explanation: Size shows the order of importance.

statement: On a sale page, the price, the product name and the delivery terms are all the same size and colour. The visual hierarchy is clear.
explanation: When everything looks the same, nothing stands out.

statement: A charity page puts its main message in large bold text at the top and the details in smaller text below. The hierarchy guides readers' eyes.
explanation: Bigger text near the top is read first.

statement: A website makes its small print bigger and brighter than its main heading. This strengthens the visual hierarchy.
explanation: It confuses the hierarchy by making minor text look most important.

statement: A shop uses a bright colour for its "Add to basket" button and for nothing else. Colour is part of the visual hierarchy here.
explanation: A unique colour signals importance.

statement: A museum's homepage hero is a tiny photo at the bottom of the page. Visitors see it first.
explanation: A hero is the large section at the top; a tiny photo at the bottom is not.

statement: An adventure holiday site's homepage hero shows a kayaker on white water with the words "Find your wild". The hero sets the tone at once.
explanation: A big image and a short message at the top create a first impression.

statement: A bakery's homepage hero is five paragraphs of text with no image. The hero grabs attention quickly.
explanation: Long text with no image is slow to read and unlikely to grab attention.

statement: A school's homepage hero changes between photos of the play, sports day and the science fair. The hero shows off different parts of school life.
explanation: Changing images highlight several key messages.

statement: A shop's homepage hero shows a product that is sold out. The hero helps the shop to sell.
explanation: Showing off a sold-out product frustrates visitors.

statement: A gym's homepage ends with a big button: "Start your free week". The call to action tells visitors exactly what to do next.
explanation: A clear CTA encourages one specific action.

statement: A charity's donation page uses "Maybe later" as its main call to action. The wording encourages people to give now.
explanation: "Maybe later" invites people to put it off.

statement: A newsletter box says "Get one recipe a week: sign up". The call to action tells visitors what they will get.
explanation: A CTA that shows the benefit is more persuasive.

statement: A shop page has seven different calls to action, all in bright colours. Visitors will know exactly which one matters most.
explanation: Too many equal CTAs compete for attention.

statement: A concert site places "Buy tickets" next to each date. The calls to action appear where fans need them.
explanation: Placing the CTA beside the information makes action easy.

statement: A website for a toddler swimming class uses dark colours, long paragraphs and technical terms. It suits its target audience of busy parents.
explanation: Busy parents need clear, short information.

statement: A skateboard brand's site uses short videos, slang and bold colours. It is designed for a teenage target audience.
explanation: These choices reflect teenage tastes.

statement: A website selling hearing aids uses tiny text and fast, noisy videos without captions. The design suits its target audience.
explanation: Its audience is likely to need large text and captions.

statement: A university site for international students offers its pages in several languages. This helps its target audience.
explanation: Translations serve visitors from different countries.

statement: A site selling luxury cars uses cheap-looking clip art and flashing discount banners. The design suits its wealthy target audience.
explanation: Cheap-looking design clashes with luxury.

statement: A café's website shows its menu in three columns on a laptop and in one column on a phone. The site uses responsive design.
explanation: It adapts the layout to the screen size.

statement: A shop's site looks the same on a phone as on a laptop, so visitors have to zoom and scroll sideways. The site uses responsive design.
explanation: A responsive site would adapt so visitors don't need to zoom.

statement: On a tablet, a news site's images shrink to fit the screen. This is part of responsive design.
explanation: Resizing content for each screen is responsive design.

statement: A school decides that responsive design isn't needed because most parents check its website on their phones.
explanation: Phone users are exactly who responsive design helps.

statement: A festival site hides its long sidebar on phones and shows it on laptops. Responsive design decides what fits each screen.
explanation: Adapting what appears suits each device.

statement: A shop puts its logo in the bottom right corner and its basket icon in the footer. The site follows common web conventions.
explanation: Convention puts the logo top left and the basket top right.

statement: Clicking a site's logo takes visitors back to the homepage. This is a common web convention.
explanation: Visitors expect the logo to link home.

statement: A website styles its links exactly like normal text. This follows the usual convention for links.
explanation: Links usually look different, often underlined or coloured.

statement: A shopping site puts the basket icon in the top right corner. Shoppers find it quickly because they expect it there.
explanation: Following conventions makes sites predictable.

statement: A designer breaks web conventions on purpose to look original. Visitors will probably find the site easier to use.
explanation: Breaking conventions makes visitors relearn how things work.

statement: A children's science site says "Let's find out why the sky is blue!" next to a cartoon rocket. The tone is friendly and excited.
explanation: "Let's", an exclamation mark and a cartoon feel playful.

statement: A hospital's website uses jokes and slang to explain a serious operation. The tone suits the subject.
explanation: A serious medical subject needs a calm, careful tone.

statement: A bank writes "Your money is safe with us" in calm, simple sentences. The tone is reassuring.
explanation: Calm, clear writing builds trust.

statement: A rock festival's site says "Attendees are requested to arrive punctually." The tone matches the festival's wild, fun image.
explanation: Formal language feels stiff, not wild or fun.

statement: A design studio's site uses short, confident sentences and bold images. The tone suggests the studio knows what it is doing.
explanation: Confident writing and bold design create an assured tone.

statement: A charity's donation button is broken, but the site looks beautiful. The site is effective at its purpose.
explanation: Looks don't matter if visitors cannot donate.

statement: After a cinema moves "Buy tickets" to the top of each film page, online sales rise. The change improved the site's effectiveness.
explanation: Rising sales show the site now achieves its purpose better.

statement: A pet shelter's site gets thousands of visitors, but almost nobody fills in its adoption form because it is too long. The site is effective.
explanation: Visitors are not adopting, so it is failing its main purpose.

statement: To judge a website's effectiveness, a designer asks whether it achieves its purpose for its target audience.
explanation: Effectiveness is about purpose and audience together.

statement: A website for older readers wins a design award for its tiny, stylish text, but older readers struggle to read it. The site is effective for its audience.
explanation: An award does not help if the audience struggles to read the site.

statement: Booking a train ticket never takes more than two minutes, and the site remembers the traveller's usual journey. The user experience is smooth.
explanation: Saving time and effort creates a good overall impression.

statement: A shop looks stunning, but its checkout crashes twice before the order goes through. The user experience is excellent.
explanation: A beautiful look cannot make up for a frustrating checkout.

statement: A streaming app suggests shows that the viewer actually enjoys. Good suggestions improve the user experience.
explanation: Feeling understood makes using the app more pleasant.

statement: A designer changes a site's colours but leaves its confusing checkout untouched, and says the user experience is now fixed.
explanation: The colours change the look; the confusing checkout still spoils the experience.

statement: A resident finds the answer to her question on a council website in under a minute and leaves satisfied. The site gave her a good user experience.
explanation: Quick success leaves a good overall impression.

statement: A banking app's UI uses tiny unlabelled buttons that look identical. Customers can tell at a glance which button sends money.
explanation: Identical, unlabelled buttons make the interface confusing.

statement: A music app redesigns its play, pause and skip buttons to be larger and clearer. This is a change to the user interface.
explanation: The UI is the visible controls people use.

statement: A company makes its servers faster. This is a change to the user interface.
explanation: Server speed is behind the scenes, not the visible controls.

statement: A map app's UI has a single search box and a "my location" button. The simple interface lets users start straight away.
explanation: A few clear controls are easy to use.

statement: A game's UI covers half the screen with menus during play. Players see the action clearly.
explanation: A crowded interface hides the game.

statement: A news site lets readers make the text larger without breaking the layout. This improves accessibility.
explanation: People with weak eyesight read comfortably.

statement: A video on a school website has no captions. Deaf parents will follow it easily.
explanation: Without captions, deaf parents miss the spoken information.

statement: Every button on a shop's site can be reached and pressed using only a keyboard. This helps people who cannot use a mouse.
explanation: Keyboard access is an important part of accessibility.

statement: A bank shows important warnings only in red text, with no words or icons to explain them. Colour-blind customers will notice them easily.
explanation: Some colour-blind people cannot pick out red, so warnings need words or icons too.

statement: Captions on a sports video help deaf fans, and they also help fans watching on a noisy bus. Good accessibility often helps everyone.
explanation: Features designed for some users often benefit many.

statement: A council website hides its "Report a problem" form four menus deep. The site has high usability for this task.
explanation: Hiding a common task makes it hard to complete.

statement: In testing, eight out of ten people pay a bill on an energy company's site without help. The site has good usability for this task.
explanation: Most people complete the task easily.

statement: A site wins praise for its beautiful animations, but users take ten minutes to find the opening times. Its usability is excellent.
explanation: Beauty does not help if simple tasks take too long.

statement: A library site lets members renew all their books with one button. This improves usability.
explanation: Fewer steps make the task easier.

statement: A form clears the whole page when a user makes a single mistake. This improves usability.
explanation: Losing everything makes the task harder.

statement: A photo app lets users pinch to zoom, just as other apps do. The control feels intuitive.
explanation: It works the way users already expect.

statement: To open the basket on a shop's site, users have to double-click the logo. The design is intuitive.
explanation: Nobody would guess that without being told.

statement: A children's game uses big arrows to show where to go next. Young players understand it without instructions.
explanation: Obvious signs make the game intuitive.

statement: A website needs a ten-page guide before visitors can find its contact form. The site is intuitive.
explanation: If it needs a long guide, it is not intuitive.

statement: An app's bin icon deletes things, as it does in most other apps. Users understand it at once.
explanation: Familiar symbols feel intuitive.

statement: A charity homepage has six images, six headings and six buttons, each the same size. The page has a clear focal point.
explanation: When everything is equal, nothing stands out.

statement: A travel site's homepage shows one huge photo of a mountain with a single bright "Explore" button on it. The button is the focal point.
explanation: One bright element on a big image draws the eye.

statement: A shop places its focal point, a bright sale banner, right over the products, so shoppers cannot see them. The focal point helps them choose products.
explanation: The banner blocks the products it should lead to.

statement: A portfolio puts the designer's best project large, in the centre of the page. The focal point shows visitors her strongest work first.
explanation: The eye goes to the largest, central item.

statement: A news page makes a flashing advert the brightest thing on the screen. Readers will probably notice the main story before the advert.
explanation: The flashing advert becomes the focal point and pulls eyes away from the story.

statement: A road-safety site uses big, plain letters for its warnings. The legibility helps drivers read them quickly.
explanation: Plain, large letters are easy to recognise.

statement: A wedding site uses a script font so decorative that the letters "l" and "t" look the same. Its legibility is high.
explanation: If letters look alike, legibility is low.

statement: On a phone, very thin letters almost disappear. A slightly bolder font improves legibility.
explanation: Thicker strokes are easier to see on small screens.

statement: A designer makes the text tiny so that more fits on the screen. This improves legibility.
explanation: Tiny text is harder to recognise.

statement: A website avoids codes that mix letters and numbers that look alike, such as the letter O and the number 0. This improves legibility.
explanation: Avoiding similar-looking characters reduces mistakes.

statement: A science site writes its articles as one huge paragraph full of long words. Readability is high.
explanation: Long, unbroken text is tiring to read.

statement: A health site breaks all its advice into short paragraphs with clear headings. This improves readability.
explanation: Short chunks are easier to read.

statement: A page uses a clear, large font but writes in long, confusing sentences. The letters are legible, but the readability is poor.
explanation: Clear letters don't help if the sentences are hard to follow.

statement: A news article's lines stretch across a whole wide screen, so readers lose their place. This improves readability.
explanation: Very long lines make it hard to find the start of the next line.

statement: An app for eight-year-olds writes its instructions in technical words. The readability suits its users.
explanation: Technical words are hard for young children.

statement: A history site adds a short quiz at the end of each article, and more readers stay to try it. The quiz increases engagement.
explanation: Taking part keeps readers involved.

statement: Visitors leave a blog after five seconds on average. The blog has high engagement.
explanation: Leaving that quickly shows low engagement.

statement: A museum app lets families collect virtual stamps at each exhibit, and they spend longer in the museum. The app boosts engagement.
explanation: A game-like feature keeps people involved.

statement: A news site fills its pages with pop-ups that block the articles. This improves engagement.
explanation: Blocking articles annoys readers and drives them away.

statement: A cooking channel asks viewers to post photos of their dishes. Many do, and they come back to see each other's. Engagement grows.
explanation: Inviting people to take part builds involvement.

statement: A page shows only text and pictures, with nothing to click, swipe or fill in. Visitors have many interactions with it.
explanation: With nothing to act on, there are no interactions.

statement: A visitor drags a slider to set a price range on a shopping site. Dragging the slider is an interaction.
explanation: The visitor acts and the site changes.

statement: A weather app updates the forecast by itself each hour while the phone sits in a pocket. This is an interaction by the user.
explanation: The user did nothing; interactions are actions the visitor takes.

statement: On a clothes site, swiping a photo shows the jacket in the next colour. The swipe is an interaction that changes what is shown.
explanation: The visitor's action changes the page.

statement: A shop's "Add to basket" button gives no sign that anything happened. Shoppers will feel confident the item was added.
explanation: Without a response, shoppers cannot tell whether it worked.

statement: After a visitor presses "Send", a green tick and "Message sent" appear. This is feedback.
explanation: It confirms what happened after the action.

statement: After paying, a customer sees a blank white screen. The site has given clear feedback.
explanation: A blank screen leaves the customer unsure whether the payment worked.

statement: A password box turns red and says "At least 8 characters" when the password is too short. The feedback helps the user fix it.
explanation: It explains the problem straight away.

statement: A download button shows no sign that anything is happening for thirty seconds. The feedback is clear.
explanation: With no sign of progress, users may click again or give up.

statement: A "Like" heart fills with colour when it is tapped. The small change is feedback that the like was counted.
explanation: A visible change confirms the action.

statement: On a laptop, a link looks exactly the same when the mouse rests on it. The link has a clear hover state.
explanation: A hover state means it changes when the pointer rests on it.

statement: A button darkens slightly when the pointer moves over it. The hover state shows that it can be clicked.
explanation: The change signals that it is interactive.

statement: A shop shows its prices only in hover states. Phone users will see the prices easily.
explanation: Phones have no hover, so phone users miss them.

statement: A gallery's thumbnails grow slightly when the mouse rests on them. The hover state invites visitors to click.
explanation: Growing on hover suggests "choose me".

statement: A menu's hover state makes the text disappear when the pointer rests on it. The hover state helps visitors read the menu.
explanation: Disappearing text makes the menu unreadable.

statement: A video made for phones is tall and narrow, but a website shows it in a wide box with black bars at the sides. The aspect ratios do not match.
explanation: Tall and wide shapes don't fit each other.

statement: A shop stretches its product photos to the same wide shape, so round plates look oval. The photos keep their aspect ratio.
explanation: Stretching changes the relationship between width and height.

statement: A gallery crops all its thumbnails to squares. A shared aspect ratio makes the grid look neat.
explanation: Shapes that match line up tidily.

statement: A trailer filmed in a very wide shape fills a tall phone screen perfectly, with no bars and no cropping.
explanation: Different aspect ratios mean it needs bars or cropping.

statement: A designer keeps a photo's aspect ratio when making it smaller. The photo shrinks without looking squashed.
explanation: Keeping the ratio keeps the shapes correct.

statement: A photographer's portfolio uses low-resolution images that look blurry on big screens. The images show her work at its best.
explanation: Blurry images hide the quality of her work.

statement: A shop offers high-resolution photos so shoppers can zoom in on the fabric. The detail helps them decide.
explanation: High resolution gives enough detail to zoom.

statement: A designer replaces small thumbnails with huge high-resolution photos. The page will probably load faster.
explanation: Higher resolution usually means bigger files, which load more slowly.

statement: A logo saved at low resolution looks fuzzy when it is printed on a large banner.
explanation: Low resolution lacks the detail needed for large sizes.

statement: A museum puts a photo of a painting online at very low resolution. Visitors will be able to zoom in and study the brushstrokes.
explanation: Low resolution lacks the detail needed for zooming.

statement: A travel blog compresses its photos to a fifth of their original file size. Its pages now load faster.
explanation: Smaller files load more quickly.

statement: A designer compresses a photo so much that it becomes blocky and smeared. The photo looks better than before.
explanation: Too much compression damages the image.

statement: Good compression is a balance: the file becomes small, but the image still looks clear.
explanation: The aim is speed without visible loss.

statement: An online shop uploads its photos straight from the camera, uncompressed. This will make its pages load quickly.
explanation: Huge uncompressed files slow pages down.

statement: A school compresses its videos before putting them online, so parents on slow connections are able to watch them.
explanation: Smaller files suit slow connections.

statement: A shop's homepage takes twelve seconds to load on a phone. Most shoppers will wait patiently.
explanation: Many people leave if a page takes that long.

statement: A news site removes three heavy adverts, and every page loads twice as fast. The shorter loading time may keep readers on the site.
explanation: Faster pages reduce frustration.

statement: A charity's office has very fast internet, so it decides that loading time doesn't matter for its website.
explanation: Its visitors may be on phones or slow connections, even if the office isn't.

statement: A recipe site shows the text first and loads the big photos just after. Visitors start reading straight away.
explanation: Showing key content first makes the wait feel shorter.

statement: A game site plays a long animation each time a page opens. This reduces loading time.
explanation: An animation adds to the wait.

statement: Before choosing any colours, a designer draws grey boxes to show where the menu, photo and text will go. This is a wireframe.
explanation: It shows structure before visual styling.

statement: A wireframe for a café's site shows the final photos, colours and fonts in full detail.
explanation: A wireframe is a simple plan without visual styling.

statement: A team uses a wireframe to agree where the "Book" button goes before anyone designs it. This saves time later.
explanation: Agreeing the structure early avoids redesigns.

statement: Customers visit a shoe shop's wireframe to buy trainers.
explanation: A wireframe is an early plan; customers use the finished site.

statement: A wireframe made of boxes and labels lets a client focus on the layout without arguing about colours.
explanation: Leaving out styling keeps attention on structure.

statement: A team builds a clickable prototype of an app but never shows it to any users. They have tested the design with users.
explanation: A prototype only tests a design with users if users try it.

statement: A clickable prototype lets testers try booking a table before the real site is built. Problems are fixed cheaply.
explanation: Testing early catches problems before building.

statement: A designer's paper sketches, which testers "tap" with a finger, cannot count as a prototype because they are not the final website.
explanation: Prototypes are test versions and can be rough, even on paper.

statement: Testers using a prototype get lost looking for the basket, so the designer moves it before the final build.
explanation: The prototype revealed a problem early.

statement: A company skips prototyping and builds the full site straight away. This will make changes cheaper later on.
explanation: Changing a finished site is usually more expensive.

statement: A news photo has the alt text "Firefighters carry a child from a flooded house". A screen reader tells blind readers what the photo shows.
explanation: Alt text describes images for screen readers.

statement: An image's alt text is "image123.jpg". The alt text describes the picture usefully.
explanation: A file name says nothing about what the image shows.

statement: A decorative swirl that adds no information is given empty alt text, so screen readers skip it.
explanation: Not every image needs a description.

statement: A shop gives each product photo the alt text "photo". Blind shoppers learn exactly what each product looks like.
explanation: "Photo" tells them nothing.

statement: Good alt text also helps search engines understand what an image shows.
explanation: Search engines read alt text too.

statement: A site has a breakpoint at 600 pixels, but nothing changes when the screen gets narrower than that. The breakpoint is working.
explanation: A working breakpoint changes the layout at that width.

statement: When the screen is narrower than 768 pixels, a magazine site switches from two columns to one. 768 pixels is a responsive breakpoint.
explanation: It is a width where the layout changes.

statement: A designer says a breakpoint makes a site change from blue to green at night.
explanation: A breakpoint is a screen width where the layout changes, not a time of day.

statement: A designer tests a site at each breakpoint to check that nothing overlaps.
explanation: Layouts change at breakpoints, so each one needs checking.

statement: A site has a single breakpoint, set for very wide TV screens. Phone users will get a layout made for them.
explanation: With no breakpoint for small screens, phones get the desktop layout.

statement: A council website reorganises its pages around what residents want to do (Pay, Report, Apply) instead of around its internal departments. This improves its information architecture.
explanation: Organising content by users' tasks helps people find where information belongs.

statement: A university website files "Fees" under "About us > History > Finance office". Students will probably find fee information where they expect it.
explanation: Burying fees under History does not match where students expect them.

statement: Before building a recipe site, a team sorts 300 recipes into categories and tests the labels with real cooks. The team is working on information architecture.
explanation: Organising and labelling content is the core of information architecture.

statement: A museum renames "Visit" as "Your Odyssey" and "Shop" as "Treasure Vault". The new labels make its information architecture clearer.
explanation: Clever labels hide where things are; familiar labels usually work better.

statement: A shop lists the same product under three unrelated menus. This leaves visitors confused about where things belong.
explanation: Inconsistent organisation weakens information architecture.

statement: A team mapping a holiday company's user journey looks just at the moment the customer presses "Pay".
explanation: A user journey covers the whole sequence, from searching to after booking.

statement: A team maps a parent's experience from first hearing about a summer camp to receiving the confirmation email. They are mapping a user journey.
explanation: It covers the full sequence of experiences towards the goal.

statement: A customer gives up halfway through renting a bike online. She has still completed the user journey.
explanation: Giving up means the journey ended before the goal was reached.

statement: A journey map shows that many customers phone the bank after using its website. This suggests the website leaves part of the journey unfinished.
explanation: Calls after visits show the site didn't fully meet their needs.

statement: Mapping a cinema's user journey, a designer stops at the moment the visitor opens the homepage. The map is complete.
explanation: The journey continues until the goal, such as buying a ticket, is achieved.
