statement: A food delivery app's user flow goes: choose a restaurant, add dishes, check the basket, pay, track the order. Each step leads to the next.
explanation: A user flow is the planned series of screens and actions for one task.

statement: A checkout's user flow sends customers back to the homepage after they enter their address. The flow is smooth.
explanation: Sending them back interrupts the task.

statement: Designers cut a sign-up flow from six screens to three, and new users finish faster.
explanation: Fewer steps make the flow simpler.

statement: After changing a site's colours, a designer calls the result a new user flow.
explanation: A user flow is a series of steps and screens; colour is styling.

statement: A flow diagram reveals a dead end: after resetting a password, users reach a page with no way forward.
explanation: Mapping the flow exposes broken steps.

statement: A form asks users to remember a code from one page and type it on the next. This reduces cognitive load.
explanation: Remembering information between pages adds mental effort.

statement: A shop shows a progress bar, "Step 2 of 4", during checkout. This lowers cognitive load because users know where they are.
explanation: Knowing the progress reduces mental effort.

statement: A homepage offers twenty equally bright options. The extra choice reduces cognitive load.
explanation: Many equal options increase the effort needed to decide.

statement: Grouping a long settings page into four labelled sections reduces cognitive load.
explanation: Chunking information makes it easier to process.

statement: An app explains every feature in one long pop-up the first time it opens. This keeps cognitive load low.
explanation: A long explanation all at once overloads new users.

statement: A button with a slight shadow looks raised, as if it could be pressed. The shadow is an affordance.
explanation: The look suggests how it can be used.

statement: A link styled as plain black text, with no underline or colour, has a strong affordance.
explanation: Nothing about it suggests it can be clicked.

statement: A slider's round handle invites users to drag it. The handle's shape provides an affordance.
explanation: Its shape suggests dragging.

statement: A flat grey box that is actually a button has a clear affordance for first-time users.
explanation: A flat grey box gives no hint that it can be pressed.

statement: In a to-do app, six small dots beside each task suggest that the task can be dragged into a new order.
explanation: The dots are a visual cue that hints at a possible action.

statement: A museum's complete homepage redesign is described as a microinteraction.
explanation: A microinteraction is a small response to one action, not a whole redesign.

statement: When a user adds an item to a wishlist, the heart icon pops and turns red. This is a microinteraction.
explanation: It is a small response connected to one action.

statement: A dark-mode toggle shows no visible change until the page is reloaded. This is a strong microinteraction.
explanation: With no immediate response, the microinteraction fails.

statement: A "Copied!" message appears for a second after a user copies a link. The microinteraction confirms the action.
explanation: It is small, quick feedback for one action.

statement: Each time a user ticks a box on a form, a five-second animation plays. This microinteraction makes the form faster to complete.
explanation: Long animations slow the form down.

statement: An airline's booking page shows only "From", "To" and "Date" at first, with "More options" for extras such as pets. This is progressive disclosure.
explanation: Essential fields come first; extras appear on request.

statement: A camera app shows every advanced setting on its main screen at once. This uses progressive disclosure.
explanation: Showing everything at once is the opposite of progressive disclosure.

statement: A recipe shows the basic method, with a "Why this works" link for curious cooks. The extra detail appears only when it is wanted.
explanation: Detail is revealed on demand.

statement: A bank hides the "Pay" button behind "More options" on its payment screen and calls this progressive disclosure.
explanation: Progressive disclosure hides extras; the button for the main task must stay visible.

statement: An FAQ page shows only the questions, and each answer opens when its question is selected. Readers scan before they read.
explanation: Revealing answers on demand keeps the page short.

statement: A warning in small grey text, surrounded by other small grey text, has high visual salience.
explanation: It does not differ from its surroundings, so its salience is low.

statement: One red button on a page of blue buttons has high visual salience.
explanation: It differs clearly from its surroundings.

statement: Every element on a page is made bright and bold. This increases the salience of the most important one.
explanation: When everything stands out, nothing does.

statement: A gently moving element on an otherwise still page catches the eye. Movement increases visual salience.
explanation: Motion makes it differ from its surroundings.

statement: A streaming service gives its "Cancel subscription" link the highest visual salience on the page. This will probably encourage customers to stay.
explanation: High salience draws people towards cancelling.

statement: A charity puts its main message and "Donate" button above the fold, so visitors see them before scrolling.
explanation: Above the fold is what is visible before scrolling.

statement: A cinema puts its film times at the very bottom of a long page. Visitors usually see them above the fold.
explanation: At the bottom, they appear only after scrolling.

statement: Because screens differ in size, the fold falls in a different place on a phone, a tablet and a laptop.
explanation: Different devices show different amounts before scrolling.

statement: A blog puts its best article below the fold. No visitor will ever see it.
explanation: Many visitors do scroll.

statement: A news app shows the top headline, an image and the first lines above the fold, inviting readers to scroll for more.
explanation: A strong start above the fold encourages scrolling.

statement: Testing a site in a wide desktop browser alone, a designer assumes every visitor's viewport is the same size. This is a safe assumption.
explanation: Viewports vary widely, especially between phones and desktops.

statement: When a user turns a tablet from upright to sideways, the viewport becomes wider.
explanation: The visible area changes shape.

statement: An image twice as wide as the viewport fits neatly on screen without scrolling or resizing.
explanation: It is wider than the visible area.

statement: A designer sets a page to fit the device's viewport, so text doesn't appear tiny on phones.
explanation: Matching the viewport sizes content correctly.

statement: Zooming in on a page lets the viewport show more of the page at once.
explanation: Zooming in shows less of the page, at a larger size.

statement: A user presses Tab to move from field to field in a form and Enter to submit it. This is keyboard navigation.
explanation: She moves and acts using keys.

statement: A site's dropdown menus open only when the mouse hovers over them. Keyboard users can open them easily.
explanation: Hover-only menus shut out keyboard users.

statement: A visible outline shows which link is selected as a keyboard user tabs through a page. The outline makes keyboard navigation possible.
explanation: Users need to see where they are.

statement: The focus outline on a news site is removed because it looks untidy. Keyboard users will still know where they are on the page.
explanation: Without the outline, they lose their place.

statement: A "Skip to main content" link at the top lets keyboard users jump past the menu.
explanation: It saves them tabbing through every menu link.

statement: Light grey text on a white background has a contrast ratio of about 1.5 to 1. This is strong enough for most readers.
explanation: 1.5 to 1 is very low contrast.

statement: Black text on white has a very high contrast ratio, about 21 to 1.
explanation: Black and white are as far apart in brightness as possible.

statement: Mid-green text is placed on a mid-red background because the colours look very different. The contrast ratio is sure to be high.
explanation: Contrast ratio measures brightness; mid-green and mid-red can be similar in brightness, giving a low ratio.

statement: A designer uses a tool to check that a button's text and background meet the minimum contrast ratio. The check helps people with weak eyesight.
explanation: Measuring the ratio helps keep text readable.

statement: A team raises the contrast ratio between text and background. This makes the page harder for people with low vision to read.
explanation: Higher contrast makes reading easier.

statement: A bakery adds "Fresh sourdough in Leeds" to its page title. This helps people searching for sourdough in Leeds to find it.
explanation: Relevant words help search engines match the page to searches.

statement: A site repeats "cheap shoes" two hundred times in hidden white text. This usually counts as good SEO practice.
explanation: Search engines penalise hidden keyword stuffing.

statement: Clear headings and alt text help both visitors and search engines understand a page. Good SEO and good design often overlap.
explanation: The same clarity serves both.

statement: A shop pays for an advert above the search results and calls this its SEO.
explanation: SEO improves a site's natural ranking; paid adverts are separate.

statement: A fast-loading, mobile-friendly site may rank higher in search results.
explanation: Search engines reward a good experience for users.

statement: A writer says the 800-word article on a webpage is the page's metadata.
explanation: Metadata describes the page; the article is its main content.

statement: A page's title and the short description shown under it in search results are metadata.
explanation: They describe the page.

statement: Each page on a large site has the same title and description. This helps search engines tell the pages apart.
explanation: Identical metadata makes pages hard to tell apart.

statement: A photo's metadata records the date it was taken and the camera used.
explanation: Metadata is information describing a file.

statement: A shop leaves the descriptions of its product pages blank. This makes the pages more attractive in search results.
explanation: Blank descriptions give searchers no reason to click.

statement: A gym's website gets 1,000 visitors and 50 sign-ups. Each sign-up is a conversion.
explanation: A conversion is a desired action completed.

statement: A visitor looks at a product and leaves without buying. This counts as a conversion for the shop.
explanation: Leaving without buying is not the desired action.

statement: After a charity shortens its donation form, its conversion rate rises from 2% to 5%.
explanation: An easier form leads more visitors to give.

statement: An advert doubles a shop's visitors, but sales stay exactly the same. Its conversion rate has improved.
explanation: More visitors with the same sales means the rate has fallen.

statement: For a newsletter, a conversion might be a sign-up; for a shop, a sale. What counts as a conversion depends on the site's purpose.
explanation: The desired action depends on the goal.

statement: A team designs a detailed desktop site first and squeezes it onto phones at the end. This is mobile-first design.
explanation: Mobile-first design starts with small screens.

statement: A café designs its site for phones first, deciding what matters most on a small screen, then adds extras for laptops.
explanation: That is the mobile-first approach.

statement: Because a festival's site was designed mobile-first, it shows a tiny phone layout in the middle of laptop screens.
explanation: Mobile-first designs expand to use larger screens well.

statement: Mobile-first design forces teams to decide what is truly essential, because space is limited.
explanation: Small screens leave room only for the most important content.

statement: A site for commuters, who mostly read on trains, is designed for large desktop screens alone. This follows a mobile-first approach.
explanation: Commuters use phones; a desktop-only design ignores them.

statement: Designers watch five teenagers try to buy concert tickets and note where they hesitate. This is user testing.
explanation: They observe real users attempting a task.

statement: A designer asks her colleagues whether they like the colours. This is user testing.
explanation: Colleagues' opinions are not observations of representative users doing tasks.

statement: User testing shows that most testers miss the "Next" button, so the team makes it larger.
explanation: Testing exposes problems the team had not seen.

statement: A team tests a children's app with adult designers and nobody else. The results show how children will use it.
explanation: Testers should represent the real users.

statement: Even testing with a handful of users often uncovers most of the major problems.
explanation: Small tests can reveal the biggest issues.

statement: The first version of a site is launched and left unchanged for years. This is an iterative process.
explanation: Iteration means repeated cycles of improvement.

statement: A team designs, tests and improves its booking page three times before launch. Each version is an iteration.
explanation: Repeated cycles produce improved versions.

statement: For its second iteration, a team throws away all its test results and starts again from a blank page.
explanation: Iterations build on what testing revealed.

statement: Version 4 of a sign-up page, after three rounds of testing, has half as many errors as version 1. Iteration has improved it.
explanation: Each cycle fixed problems.

statement: A company tests its prototype, ignores the results and launches it unchanged. It has completed an iteration.
explanation: An iteration needs the results to shape an improved version.

statement: A design brief for a bakery says: "Purpose: take online orders. Audience: local families. Must work on phones. Budget: £2,000." It sets out what the site must do.
explanation: A brief sets out purpose, audience, requirements and constraints.

statement: A client sends a designer the finished, working website and calls it the design brief.
explanation: A brief is a statement of what the site must achieve, written before the design.

statement: A designer checks her homepage against the brief and notices that it ignores the brief's target audience of older readers.
explanation: The brief guides and tests design decisions.

statement: A brief that says only "Make it look nice" gives a designer clear direction.
explanation: It gives no purpose, audience or requirements.

statement: An agreed design brief prevents many arguments later, because everyone accepted the goals at the start.
explanation: A shared brief keeps the team aligned.

statement: A client's budget of £500 is not a constraint on the design.
explanation: A budget limits what can be built.

statement: A site must work on old school laptops with slow internet. This is a constraint the designer must work within.
explanation: It limits the technology and file sizes.

statement: A designer ignores the brief's constraint that the site must be ready in two weeks and plans a six-month project. The plan fits the brief.
explanation: It breaks the time constraint.

statement: Designing for a small phone screen is a constraint that forces the designer to choose only essential content.
explanation: Screen size limits what fits.

statement: According to one designer, a brief's strict two-colour limit can only make a site worse.
explanation: Limits often make a design more focused and distinctive.
